steps.title: Wireless Magic: The 13.56 MHz RFID Transceiver
steps.markdownContent:
### Contactless Identification for Secret Agent Monsters
Have you ever tapped a plastic keycard against a hotel room door, scanned an automated subway pass, or used contactless tap-to-pay with a phone? These systems use **RFID (Radio-Frequency Identification)**!

In our monster robotics lab, we want our monster access gate to identify authorized monster operators instantly by reading secret digital tokens. To do this, we use the **RC522 RFID Module** (`comp_23`).

```
RC522 Reader (Active Transmitter)                 Smart Card / Key Fob (Passive Tag)
┌────────────────────────────────┐                 ┌────────────────────────────────┐
│ [MFRC522 IC]                   │                 │ Microscopic Silicon Chip       │
│       │                        │  13.56 MHz RF   │       ▲                        │
│ [Copper PCB Loop Antenna]      │════ Magnetic ═══►│ [Internal Wire Coil Antenna]   │
│ Transmits 13.56 MHz EM Field   │     Field       │ Powered by Inductive Coupling! │
└────────────────────────────────┘                 └────────────────────────────────┘
```

### The Mystery of the Batteryless Card
Look closely at your blue RFID keychain fob and white plastic access card. They have **no batteries**, no charging ports, and no solar panels! How can a dead piece of plastic compute numbers and transmit radio waves?

1. **Electromagnetic Inductive Coupling:** The RC522 reader pumps high-frequency alternating current through the wide copper trace spiraling around its circuit board, creating a localized 13.56 MHz magnetic field.
2. **Wireless Harvesting:** When you bring a card within 3 centimeters of the reader, the magnetic field cuts across a tiny coiled antenna embedded inside the plastic card.
3. **Faraday's Law of Induction:** The fluctuating magnetic field induces an electrical current in the tag's coil! A tiny internal capacitor rectifies this electricity, powering up the tag's microchip.
4. **Load Modulation:** The tag wakes up, reads its burned-in **Unique Identifier (UID)**, and alters the electrical load on its coil to transmit its secret serial number back to the RC522!

quickCheck.question: How do passive RFID cards and key fobs obtain electrical power to transmit their data back to the RC522 reader?
options: Through electromagnetic induction: the reader's 13.56 MHz magnetic field induces an electrical current inside the card's internal coil antenna
They contain miniature nuclear batteries that last 50 years
They absorb light through microscopic solar cells hidden under the plastic
quickCheck.explanation: Faraday's Law of Induction allows the reader's alternating magnetic field to transfer electrical energy wirelessly across the air gap.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Remember electromagnetism: a changing magnetic field induces an electric voltage in any nearby coil of wire.

quickCheck.question: What radio frequency standard does the MFRC522 RFID reader module operate at?
quickCheck.explanation: The RC522 conforms to ISO/IEC 14443A standard, operating at the global 13.56 MHz High Frequency Near-Field band.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Look at the component specifications for comp_23: it specifically targets 13.56 MHz smart cards.

steps.title: Inductive Coupling Physics & 3.3V Power Safety
steps.markdownContent:
### CRITICAL HARDWARE SAFETY: The 3.3V Power & Logic Rule
> [!CAUTION]
> **THE RC522 MODULE RUNS ON 3.3V POWER AND REQUIRES 3.3V LOGIC SIGNALS!**
> The MFRC522 silicon chip is rated for a maximum supply voltage of **3.6V** ($V_{DD} \le 3.6\text{V}$) and maximum input pin voltage of **$V_{DD} + 0.5\text{V} \approx 3.8\text{V}$**.
> 1. Connecting the module's `3.3V` power pin to the Arduino's `5V` power rail will **permanently destroy the internal radio receiver circuitry**! Always connect the module's power pin strictly to the Uno's **3.3V** pin.
> 2. The Arduino Uno's digital output pins emit **5V logic**! Connecting Uno 5V outputs (`MOSI`, `SCK`, `SS/CS`, `RST`) directly to the 3.3V RC522 inputs overstresses its input protection diodes. Unless using a breakout board with built-in level-shifter circuitry, use a **bidirectional logic level shifter** or **voltage divider** (e.g., $1\,\text{k}\Omega$ in series from Uno pin, tapped to RC522 input with $2\,\text{k}\Omega$ to GND) on each 5V output signal line!
> 3. The `MISO` line (RC522 $\to$ Uno Pin 12) outputs 3.3V logic, which safely exceeds the ATmega328P minimum digital HIGH input threshold ($V_{IH} \approx 3.0\text{V}$), so it can connect directly back to Uno Pin 12.

### The 8-Pin RC522 Header Pinout & Level-Shifting Architecture
```
RC522 MODULE PINOUT (8 PINS):
  1. 3.3V  ───► Connect to Uno 3.3V ONLY! (Red wire)
  2. RST   ───► Reset input: 5V Uno Pin 9 via Level Shifter / Divider ──► RC522 RST (White)
  3. GND   ───► Ground: Connect to Uno GND (Black wire)
  4. IRQ   ───► Interrupt: Leave UNCONNECTED for basic polling
  5. MISO  ───► SPI Data In: 3.3V direct to Uno Pin 12 (Yellow wire)
  6. MOSI  ───► SPI Data Out: 5V Uno Pin 11 via Level Shifter / Divider ──► RC522 MOSI (Blue)
  7. SCK   ───► SPI Clock: 5V Uno Pin 13 via Level Shifter / Divider ──► RC522 SCK (Green)
  8. SDA   ───► Chip Select (NSS/CS): 5V Uno Pin 10 via Level Shifter / Divider ──► RC522 SDA (Orange)
```

*(Note: On the RC522 module silk-screen, the Chip Select pin is labeled `SDA` or `NSS`. In SPI mode, this functions as the standard active-low `CS` line!)*

### Essential Pre-Power Verification Checklist:
- [ ] Power disconnected: USB cable unplugged from computer.
- [ ] RC522 VCC connects to **3.3V pin**, NOT 5V.
- [ ] Signal lines from Uno (Pins 9, 10, 11, 13) pass through logic level converter / resistor dividers.
- [ ] Common ground established between Uno GND and RC522 GND.
- [ ] Only after all wiring is double-checked, reconnect USB power.

interactiveConfig.question: What catastrophic mistake must you avoid when wiring power to the RC522 RFID module?
options: Connecting VCC to 5V instead of 3.3V, which will permanently destroy the MFRC522 silicon
Using a red wire instead of a green wire
Connecting ground to the Arduino GND pin
interactiveConfig.explanation: The MFRC522 chip is designed strictly for 3.3V operation. Applying 5V exceeds maximum voltage ratings and fries the silicon.

questions.explanation: The MFRC522 chip is designed strictly for 3.3V operation. Applying 5V exceeds maximum voltage ratings and fries the silicon.

questions.question: What label is standardly printed on the RC522 module header for its active-low SPI Chip Select pin?
questions.explanation: On RC522 boards, the Chip Select pin is silk-screened as SDA or NSS (Negative Slave Select).

questions.question: What is the UID read from an RFID tag by the MFRC522 library?
options: A factory-programmed Unique Identifier code that distinguishes each tag from all others
The current temperature of the card
The remaining battery voltage of the key fob
questions.explanation: The UID (Unique Identifier) is a permanent digital serial number burned into the tag's silicon chip during manufacturing.
